issues.problem: The XOR plate shows THAT the rule fails, never WHAT was shown or WHY. The main try boxes carry a glyph of each shape (— ✕, | ✕), but the XOR try boxes carry only ✓ and ✗. A 15-year-old cannot tell which of the four cases (neither, top, bottom, both) each try was. The plate also never says 'one layer'. Claim limit-linear's caveat is that the limit belongs to the single-layer machine, and the Mark I itself had a random association layer. As it stands, an expert can read 'It could learn only simple patterns … XOR never settles' as a claim about the whole Mark I and about neural networks in general.
issues.fix: Keep the real trainXor() run. (1) Give each XOR try box a tiny two-dot glyph of its case (○○ ●○ ○● ●●) before its ✓ or ✗, matching the main row's style. (2) Under the 'XOR · one lit, not both' caption, add a second line in the same face: 'one layer of dials'. (3) Optional depth beat, only if it is true in the actual run: the first time the run gets the both-lit case wrong, show the two lit dials' tugs adding past the threshold tick (two small arc arrows stacking), so the viewer sees why. Two tugs that each say yes say yes together. This is the linear-separability intuition with no algebra. Hold to the existing beats; no narration change (runtime is 67.75 s against the 68 s cap).

issues.problem: The lineage payoff is still too faint to teach. Invent no modern specifics: lineage-mlp supports multilayer, nothing more.

best_moments: ch01-s03, 55.0-58.4 s: on 'showed just how simple', a separate two-cell XOR mini machine runs Rosenblatt's rule for real. Its try row flips ✓ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗, 'never settles' is set below it, and the success plates dim beside it. The limit is now shown, not told, and it is honest: it is not hand-animated and not run on the 64-unit board.
ch01-s03, 32.7-33.1 s: 'the total decides'. The threshold label sits over the centre tick and the needle commits to VERTICAL. The weighted sum plus threshold is on screen in one beat.

ch01-s03, 36.3-39.7 s: 'motors nudge the dials that had a say'. Only the dials fed by lit cells turn, with arc arrows toward the faint target, and the 'correct answer: horizontal' tag is now clear of the try row. This is the true error-correction rule and its supervision in one uncluttered picture.
ch01-s03, 41.1-46.2 s: 'Wrong' (try 2), 'wrong again' (try 3) and 'right' (try 4, the lantern flares). The narration counts the run's real verdicts.

ch01-s03, 47.0-48.0 s: 'try 5 · a new horizontal bar · said horizontal · RIGHT' over 'THEN try 1 · a horizontal bar · said vertical · WRONG'. Labelling the new bar as a different shape is honest, and it teaches generalisation, not memorisation.

ch01-s03, 52.07 s: '1969' types on as it is spoken, set as 'Minsky & Papert, Perceptrons' with an italic title and a closed-book prop. Belief, dissent and decline fit into one sentence with no causal overclaim.
